title: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate · Units 97–98
description: Essay organisation, viewpoints, argument balance, comparison, generalisation, cause and effect, and formal letter/email vocabulary with polite correspondence conventions.

units.title: Unit 97 — Writing an essay
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 200–201 (PDF pages 201–202).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Essay writing, argument structure, contrast, generalisation, cause and effect
learningObjectives: Organise a discursive essay using a clear point of view and both sides of an argument.
Use personal and less direct ways of presenting opinions in academic-style writing.
Present advantages and disadvantages using appropriate contrasting linkers.
Compare the past and present and make cautious generalisations.
Show causes, results and consequences accurately, distinguishing the verb affect from the noun effect.
Apply the linking language in short original essay sentences and paragraphs.

items.pt: redação dissertativa; ensaio que discute um tema
items.example: A discursive essay should explore the question from several angles.
items.note: A piece of writing that discusses a subject and presents arguments, rather than just telling a story.

items.example: The final paragraph makes the writer's point of view clear.
items.note: A person's opinion or way of thinking about a question.

items.pt: os dois lados de uma argumentação
items.example: A balanced essay explains both sides of an argument.
items.note: Consider reasons for an idea as well as reasons against it.

items.example: The writer supports each argument with an example.
items.note: Here argument means a reason supporting a position, not necessarily an angry disagreement.

items.pt: palavras e expressões de ligação; conectores
items.example: Link words and phrases help readers follow your ideas.
items.note: Connectors show relationships such as addition, contrast, and result.

items.example: You can express a point of view without using strong language.
items.note: An essay-writing action: communicate an opinion clearly.

items.example: Some people believe that cities should have more parks.
items.note: Follow with a that-clause; it presents an opinion without attributing it to the writer.

items.pt: há um argumento; há motivos para defender uma ideia
items.example: There is an argument that public transport should be cheaper.
items.note: Often followed by that + a complete clause; a relatively impersonal way to state a view.

items.example: I believe that schools should teach practical skills.
items.note: Personal opinion marker; it can be followed by that + clause.

items.example: It seems to me that the proposal needs more research.
items.note: Use it seems to me that + clause; include the preposition to.

items.example: In my opinion, the course should include more discussion.
items.note: A direct personal opinion marker; the book suggests that less direct formulations can be preferable in written essays.

items.example: One of the advantages of cycling is that it costs very little.
items.note: Follow of with a noun or -ing form; often continue with is that + clause.

items.example: A major advantage of online courses is their flexibility.
items.note: A positive feature of an option; contrast with disadvantage.

items.example: One disadvantage of travelling by car is the cost of parking.
items.note: A negative feature, often compared with an advantage in discursive writing.

items.example: The course is demanding. However, it is extremely useful.
items.note: Introduces a contrast between ideas; usually separated from the following clause by a comma in this position.

items.example: On the one hand, online meetings save travel time.
items.note: Normally used with on the other hand to present contrasting points.

items.example: On the other hand, meeting in person may be more effective.
items.note: Contrasts with the first viewpoint; use hand, not side, in this expression.

items.example: The essay makes comparisons between city and rural life.
items.note: Use make comparisons between two people, periods or groups.

items.example: Compared with last year, our energy use is lower.
items.note: Introduces a comparison; compared to is also possible in this use.

items.example: Compared to my old laptop, this one is much faster.
items.note: An alternative to compared with for comparing two things.

items.example: In the past, people wrote more personal letters.
items.note: Sets up a contrast with life now; often paired with nowadays.

items.example: Nowadays, many students use digital textbooks.
items.note: Refers to the present compared with the past; not the same as the single word today in every context.

items.example: Trains are efficient in the city. In contrast, buses reach smaller villages.
items.note: Links two unlike facts or situations; in contrast to can introduce a noun phrase.

items.example: Access to higher education varies across the developed world.
items.note: A broad socioeconomic term used in the book's comparison example; its meaning depends on how development is defined.

items.example: A careful generalisation does not claim that everyone is the same.
items.note: A statement about what is usually true, not an absolute rule.

items.example: Writers sometimes make a generalisation to describe a common trend.
items.note: A useful essay-writing action; use cautious language to avoid overstatement.

items.example: In general, children enjoy learning through games.
items.note: Signals a broad pattern with possible exceptions.

items.example: On the whole, the new timetable has worked well.
items.note: Close in meaning to in general; avoids an absolute claim.

items.example: Young people tend to learn new software quickly.
items.note: Tend to + base verb expresses what usually happens, without claiming it always happens.

items.example: The conclusion explains the cause and effect of the change.
items.note: A relationship in which one event or situation produces another.

items.example: Poor planning was a major cause of the delay.
items.note: Noun: a reason why something happens; often cause of + noun.

items.example: Lack of sleep can cause concentration problems.
items.note: Verb: make something happen; this construction directly takes an object.

items.example: The improvement was the result of regular practice.
items.note: A result is what happens because of a cause; follow result of with a noun or -ing form.

items.example: The roads were flooded. Consequently, the event was cancelled.
items.note: A relatively formal linker signalling a result; often separated by a comma.

items.example: Fewer people applied and, as a result, the company changed its plans.
items.note: A result linker similar to consequently.

items.example: Regular breaks can have an effect on concentration.
items.note: Use the noun effect after an; follow with the preposition on.

items.example: Excessive noise can have a bad effect on sleep.
items.note: A phrase for a harmful consequence; distinguish the noun effect from the verb affect.

items.example: Rising prices affect families with limited incomes.
items.note: Verb meaning influence or change; do not confuse with the noun effect.

items.example: The policy had a positive effect on road safety.
items.note: Noun meaning a consequence or influence; common construction: have an effect on.

items.example: The library provides books. In addition, it offers free computer access.
items.note: Connects supporting or additional information; also taught in the book's linking-language units.

items.example: There is an argument for making public transport more accessible.
items.note: Follow argument for with a noun or -ing form; useful in the practice essay about policy choices.

items.example: The report was based on unreliable information.
items.note: Used in the practice essay to judge information that may not be accurate.

items.example: Some of the advice on that website is out-of-date.
items.note: An adjective for information that is no longer current.

sectionsChecked: A: The basis of a discursive essay, point of view and both sides of an argument
B: Expressing a point of view, including the language-help box on personal and impersonal opinions
C: Giving both sides of an argument and on the one hand / on the other hand
D: Comparing and contrasting the past and the present
E: Making generalisations through in general, on the whole and tend to
F: Cause and effect, including the affect/effect language-help box
Exercises 97.1–97.5: argument-function matching, missing words, choice of linkers, short essay completion and paraphrasing

units.title: Unit 98 — Formal letters and emails
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 202–203 (PDF pages 203–204).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Formal correspondence, openings, endings, enquiries, applications and apologies
learningObjectives: Choose appropriate greetings and sign-offs for formal letters and emails according to whether the recipient is named.
Use standard opening, request and closing formulas for formal correspondence.
Recognise vocabulary for job advertisements, graduate schemes, applications and interviews.
Enquire politely, request further details, confirm arrangements and refer to attached or enclosed documents.
Communicate positive and negative information and apologise appropriately in writing.
Proofread formal correspondence for register, spelling, prepositions and verb constructions.

items.example: She wrote a formal letter to request more information.
items.note: Uses a suitable greeting, clear purpose and appropriate closing.

items.example: A formal email should use polite and accurate language.
items.note: A formal email can follow many conventions of a formal letter.

items.example: She began her enquiry with Dear Sir or Madam because she did not know the recipient's name.
items.note: Use when the recipient's name is unknown; the traditional matching ending in British formal correspondence is Yours faithfully.

items.example: The letter to the manager began with Dear Mr Wilson.
items.note: A formal greeting followed by the man's surname; a named recipient usually takes Yours sincerely.

items.example: I am writing to ask for information about the course.
items.note: Common way to open a formal letter; usually followed by to + verb or in response to + noun.

items.example: I am writing in response to your recent advertisement.
items.note: Formal phrase meaning in reply to; the preposition is to, not with.

items.example: I saw your advertisement for graduate positions.
items.note: A public notice or promotion, including a notice about a job.

items.example: The company welcomes applications from recent graduates.
items.note: As a noun, someone who has completed a university degree.

items.example: She applied to a graduate training scheme at an engineering firm.
items.note: A structured work-training programme for people who have completed university.

items.example: He has a university degree in economics.
items.note: A higher-education qualification; the example letter refers to completing one.

items.example: I would be grateful if you could reply this week.
items.note: A very polite request formula, usually followed by if you could + base verb.

items.example: Could you send me further details about the timetable?
items.note: A formal or neutral request for more information; details is plural here.

items.example: I am available for interview on Thursday morning.
items.note: Available means free or able to attend at a particular time.

items.word: I look forward to hearing from you
items.pt: aguardo seu retorno; espero receber sua resposta
items.example: I look forward to hearing from you about the application.
items.note: Formal closing when a reply is expected; use look forward to + -ing, not to + base verb.

items.pt: atenciosamente; fórmula de despedida formal sem nome do destinatário
items.example: She closed the letter with Yours faithfully because she did not know the addressee's name.
items.note: Traditional British formal sign-off when the letter begins Dear Sir or Madam.

items.pt: atenciosamente; despedida formal com destinatário identificado
items.example: The letter began Dear Ms Taylor and ended Yours sincerely.
items.note: Traditional British formal sign-off when writing to someone whose name is known.

items.example: He ended his professional email with Kind regards.
items.note: A polite closing that works in many professional emails and letters.

items.example: Please add your signature at the bottom of the form.
items.note: The particular way someone writes their name by hand.

items.example: Please sign your name before submitting the letter.
items.note: Write your signature; the source letter shows a signature above the printed name.

items.pt: escrever o nome em letra de forma
items.example: After signing, print your name so that it is easy to read.
items.note: Print means write the name clearly in ordinary letters rather than use a handwritten signature.

items.pt: obrigado por sua carta; agradecemos sua carta
items.example: Thank you for your letter about the training programme.
items.note: A courteous way to acknowledge an earlier written message.

items.example: I am writing regarding the date of the interview.
items.note: More formal alternative to about; followed by a noun or -ing form.

items.example: I regret to inform you that the course is full.
items.note: Formal expression for disappointing news; followed by that + clause.

items.example: We received your application for the training programme.
items.note: An official request, such as a request for a job or place on a course.

items.example: Her application was successful, and she got the position.
items.note: A successful application is accepted; an unsuccessful application is rejected.

items.word: I am pleased to inform you
items.pt: tenho o prazer de informar; temos o prazer de informar
items.example: I am pleased to inform you that your place has been confirmed.
items.note: Formal expression for giving good news; commonly followed by that + clause.

items.example: I would like to enquire about evening classes.
items.note: Formal British-English spelling of inquire about; followed by a noun or -ing form.

items.pt: escrevo para solicitar informações; entro em contato para consultar
items.example: I am writing to enquire about the next available course.
items.note: A conventional formal opening; typically followed by about + noun.

items.example: Please confirm the booking before Friday.
items.note: Make a previously discussed reservation definite.

items.example: Could you confirm the revised date in writing?
items.note: Means through a written letter, email or other document, not only spoken words.

items.example: Thank you for offering your support during the event.
items.note: A polite expression for giving help or assistance.

items.word: We would like to thank you
items.pt: gostaríamos de agradecer-lhe; gostaríamos de agradecer a vocês
items.example: We would like to thank you for your patience.
items.note: Formal and polite expression of gratitude; usually followed by for + noun or -ing.

items.example: We apologise for the delay in sending your order.
items.note: Formal apology; follow for with a noun or an -ing form. British spelling: apologise.

items.pt: pedimos que aceite nossas desculpas; pedimos desculpas
items.example: Please accept our apologies for the inconvenience.
items.note: Particularly formal written apology; often followed by for + noun.

items.example: There has been a delay in processing the applications.
items.note: A situation in which something happens later than expected; can be a noun or verb.

items.pt: envio em anexo; incluo junto à carta
items.example: I enclose a copy of the signed agreement.
items.note: Traditional wording for including a document or item with a physical letter; email attachments are often introduced with I have attached.

items.example: The customer enclosed a cheque with the letter.
items.note: British-English spelling of the payment document; American spelling is check.

items.example: I am writing in reply to your message from Monday.
items.note: Similar to in response to; followed by a noun phrase.

items.example: The company invited several trainees to join its new programme.
items.note: A person receiving practical training for a role; used in the email-editing exercise.

items.example: I enclose a copy of my CV for your consideration.
items.note: An appropriate object of enclose in a paper job application; in email, attach is usually preferable.

items.example: We apologise for any inconvenience caused by the disruption.
items.note: A difficulty or problem someone experiences; used in the apology exercise.

items.word: delays of up to four weeks
items.example: Customers may experience delays of up to four weeks.
items.note: Up to introduces a maximum duration or quantity; the source complaint-response exercise uses this structure.
